newsitem.title: USA: Long-bond, holiday absentees rattle U.S. stocks.
newsitem.headline: Long-bond, holiday absentees rattle U.S. stocks.

text.p: Rising bond yields and thinly-staffed trading desks paved the way for sell programs to jolt U.S. equity markets with sharp losses Thursday, according to traders and market strategists.
While the Dow Jones Industrial average finished with a 140 point loss to 6741, it managed to rise from the session low 6664, a 217 point deficit.
A possible rebound Monday will be dictated largely by the direction of bonds, whose sharp decline in a holiday-shortened trading session sapped the appeal of stocks, they said.
Also, the market may firm Monday with all hands on deck after the Easter holiday weekend, which includes Good Friday's market close, they added.

"Once the (30-year Treasury) bond yield got above the seven percent level, it set off the sell programs and a lot of players were not here or left early," said Brad Weekes, Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette managing director.
The yield on the 30-year treasury rose to 7.09 percent Thursday after the price tumbled 1-8/32 to 94.10.
"It was a fragmented market, with wild swings and light volume of 481 million (shares traded), though it was a broad sell-off," Weekes said.

Weekes cited the wide trading range of Dow Jones Industrial components J.P. Morgan, which closed at 102-3/4, off 2-3/4, but above the session-low 98-5/8, and General Electric Co, which ended with a 2-5/8 loss to 101-1/4, up from the intraday low 99-3/8.
"I think the market is in for a tough time for a while. As long as the long end (of Treasury bond yields) stays above seven percent, it becomes a very competitive vehicle versus stocks," Weekes said.
Jim Weiss, deputy chief investment officer for equities at State Street Research, agreed that much of the market loss was tied to the long bond penetrating a seven percent yield.
"The linkage between the stock and bond markets had been suspended since last November," he said. "The linkage is now coming back into play. The long bond behaved very badly today.
"Many stock traders were not at their desks after 11 a.m. because of the three-day holiday and that caused illiquidity in the stock market."
Interviewed outside the New York Stock Exchange after the closing bell, traders were generally unshaken by the decline.
"The markets had been up so much, it's been expected. Trees don't grow to heaven," a NYSE trader said.
Said another: "It's pretty calm. We've seen it before."
A third added: "It was orderly. I think they'll walk it down a little more."
Brian Finnerty, senior vice president at Unterberg Harris said: "Monday will be a better test of the market's attitude, since trading was so light today. Things could probably come back on Monday."
